title: Road Signs Around the World
description: Red rings, blue discs, upside-down triangles: road signs are a picture language shared by the 75 countries that have joined the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals. Learn to read a sign's shape and colour before its symbol, spot the rules that are easy to miss, and meet the countries that do things their own way, from Sweden's yellow moose to Japan's triangular STOP. A travel companion to *Hello, Goodbye, and Thank You Around the World*. The rules follow the consolidated 1968 text. A 2025 amendment gives the signs new numbers from 12 November 2026.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: You don't recognise the picture inside this sign. What does the shape alone tell you?

images.alt: A white triangle, point up, with a thick red border. Inside, a small black car tilts with one side dropping off the edge of the road.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-8-V1.svg).

options.text: A hazard lies ahead, so slow down and look for it
Something is prohibited from this point on
You must do what the picture shows
A service or facility is nearby

questions.explanation: The Convention puts shape and colour first and pictures second, so drivers can understand signs in other countries (Article 8). A triangle standing on its base, with a red border and a white or yellow background, is always a **danger warning**. It gives you information, not an order. This one warns of dangerous shoulders: the edge of the road is soft or drops away. Even if the picture means nothing to you, the triangle tells you enough to slow down and watch the road.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does a white disc with a wide red ring tell you, whatever is drawn inside it?

images.alt: A white disc with a wide red ring. A red diagonal bar crosses a black tractor silhouette.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C3l-V1-1.svg).

options.text: Something is prohibited or restricted
The road ahead is dangerous for the thing shown
This route is compulsory for the thing shown
The thing shown can be found nearby

questions.explanation: Signs that ban or restrict something are round, with a white or yellow background and a **wide red border**. If there's a diagonal bar, it's red too and slopes down from left to right. This one bans tractors and other power-driven farm vehicles, but the ring said "no" before you even noticed the tractor. By the same logic, a number inside a red ring is a *maximum*: a limit you must not go over.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Which family of signs does a solid blue disc with a white symbol belong to?

images.alt: A solid blue disc with a white silhouette of a person riding a horse.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D6a.svg).

options.text: Mandatory signs: you must do this, or the way is reserved for it
Information signs: a facility is nearby
Prohibitory signs: the thing shown is banned
Warning signs: watch out for the thing shown

questions.explanation: Blue discs are **mandatory** signs: they tell you what you must do or which way you must go. This one marks a compulsory track for horse riders. Only riders may use it, and when it runs alongside the road, riders must take it. Think of it as the opposite of the red ring. A horse in a red ring bans riders; a horse on a blue disc gives them their own path.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Which shapes does the Convention use for just one sign each?
questions.description: Most shapes cover a whole family of signs. A few belong to a single sign.

options.text: A triangle pointing down
An octagon
A triangle pointing up
A circle
A square standing on one corner

questions.explanation: The downward triangle is used only for **Give Way**, and the octagon only for **STOP**. The shape says it all, which is why the Give Way sign has nothing inside. The other shapes are shared. Upward triangles cover dozens of hazards, and circles hold every prohibition and most mandatory signs. The square standing on its corner has two jobs: with a yellow centre it marks a priority road, and as a yellow diamond it is the Convention's alternative design for warning signs.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does this sign warn you about?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a black X-shaped cross in the middle.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-18a-V1.svg).

options.text: An intersection where the country's general priority rule applies
A railway level crossing
An intersection where you have priority
A junction where every driver must stop

questions.explanation: The X warns of an intersection with no special priority arrangement, so the country's **general priority rule** decides who goes first. In most of continental Europe, where traffic drives on the right, that rule is priority to the right: a car coming from your right goes first. People often take the X for a railway sign. The railway cross looks different: it's a large red-and-white cross standing on its own beside the tracks, not a black symbol inside a triangle.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: The bold vertical bar in this sign is your road. What does the thin crossbar tell you?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle containing a thick black vertical bar with pointed ends, crossed by a thinner horizontal bar.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-19a-V1.svg).

options.text: Drivers on the side road must give way to you
You must give way to the side road
The side road is closed to traffic
Priority to the right applies at the junction

questions.explanation: Thicker means more important. The thick bar is the road with priority, and the thin bar is the side road whose drivers must give way. The Convention allows this sign only where the side roads have Give Way or STOP signs, or are tracks whose drivers must give way anyway. Compare the plain X, which gives nobody priority. Even with priority, keep an eye out for drivers who ignore their sign.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What is this warning sign telling you, rather urgently?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle. A black car tips forward off the edge of a raised platform toward wavy lines of water.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-6-V1.svg).

options.text: The road leads onto a quay or river bank
A ford: the road runs through shallow water
A car ferry terminal is ahead
The road may flood after heavy rain

questions.explanation: This sign warns that the road leads onto a **quay or river bank**. The picture shows what happens if you ignore it: keep driving and you end up in the water. The Convention has no signs for fords, ferries, or flooding. Countries that need them can design their own, as long as the new sign fits the system and doesn't reuse a meaning the Convention already gives to another sign.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Why would a warning sign show a windsock?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a striped windsock on a pole, blowing out sideways.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-31-V1-1.svg).

options.text: Strong cross-winds often hit this stretch of road
An airfield is nearby
Wind turbines are being built next to the road
Service area ahead with a weather station

questions.explanation: The windsock warns that **strong cross-winds** are common on this stretch of road. A sudden gust can push tall vans, caravans, and motorcycles sideways, so hold the wheel firmly and leave room on both sides. Guessing an airfield makes sense, since that's where windsocks usually live, but the Convention has its own symbol for that: a plane flying low over the road.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: This sign says 10%. How many metres does the road drop for every 100 metres you travel horizontally?
questions.description: Answer with a number of metres.

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle. A black wedge slopes down from left to right, labelled 10%.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-2a-V1-1.svg).

questions.explanation: The number is the slope as a **percentage**: how far the road drops for the distance you travel horizontally, times 100. So a 10% descent drops 10 m for every 100 m. The Convention also lets countries write it as a ratio, 1:10. It isn't an angle: 10% is only about 5.7 degrees, and a 45-degree slope would be 100%. On a long 10% descent, shift to a lower gear so your brakes don't overheat.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Why does this Swedish sign show a moose when the Convention's example shows a deer?

images.alt: A triangle with a red border and a yellow background, showing a black silhouette of a moose.
images.caption: Swedish road sign A19. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sweden_road_sign_A19-1.svg).

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a black leaping deer.
images.caption: The Convention's example of a wild-animal warning uses a deer. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-15b-V1.svg).

options.text: The Convention tells each country to draw the animal drivers most often meet
Sweden opted out of the Convention's animal-warning rules
The moose sign is a tourist souvenir, not an official sign
The deer symbol is reserved for farm animals

questions.explanation: The animal warning should show the animal, domestic or wild, that drivers **meet most often** in that area. The Convention's deer and cow are just examples. Sweden has signs for moose, deer, wild boar, reindeer, and more. The yellow background is allowed too, since warning triangles may be white or yellow inside. Sweden chose yellow so its signs stay visible against winter snow.
questions.references:
[United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

[Wikipedia: Road signs in Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_signs_in_Sweden)

questions.title: What does a steam locomotive on a warning sign tell you about the railway crossing ahead?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle containing a black steam locomotive puffing smoke.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-26a-V1.svg).

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle containing a black fence of vertical bars.
images.caption: The fence symbol warns of a level crossing with gates or half-gates. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-25-V1.svg).

options.text: The crossing has no gates or barriers
Heritage steam trains run on this line
The crossing has full barriers
A railway museum is nearby

questions.explanation: The Convention has two kinds of level-crossing warning. A **fence** means the crossing has gates or half-gates. A **locomotive** is for all other level crossings, where there may be no barrier to stop you. The steam engine is just the standard picture and says nothing about how old the trains are. When you see it, look both ways and listen.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: This red-and-white cross stands right beside the tracks. What does the extra chevron below it add?

images.alt: A large red-and-white X-shaped cross with a matching red-and-white chevron directly underneath it.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_A-28b-V1-1.svg).

options.text: The line has at least two tracks
The crossing has half-barriers
The tracks cross the road at an angle
Trams, not trains, use the crossing

questions.explanation: This X, called a St Andrew's cross, stands **at** level crossings without gates or half-gates. The version with the extra chevron may be used only where the railway has **at least two tracks**. That matters because a second train can come along the other track, hidden behind the first. The Convention wants the cross to be big, with arms at least 1.2 m long, and lets it be turned on end where space is tight.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: As you approach a level crossing, you pass a panel with three red bars, then one with two. How many bars does the last panel before the tracks have?

images.alt: A tall white rectangular panel with three red diagonal bars.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-29a-V1-1.svg).

images.alt: A tall white rectangular panel with a single red diagonal bar.
images.caption: The one-bar panel stands about two-thirds of the way from the first sign to the crossing. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-29c-V1-1.svg).

questions.explanation: The panels count down. Three bars sit under the warning sign, two bars stand about a third of the way to the railway, and **one bar** stands about two-thirds of the way. The bars slope down toward the road. On fast roads, where it's hard to judge how far away a crossing is, the countdown shows you. The same panels can also appear before swing bridges.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: The exclamation-mark sign covers any danger not listed elsewhere. Which unusual case does the Convention name for it?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a large black exclamation mark.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-32-V1.svg).

options.text: A track where very slow trains are guided across the road by a railway worker giving hand signals
A stretch of road with no mobile phone signal
A road where drivers often fall asleep
A bend too complex for the ordinary bend symbols

questions.explanation: The "other dangers" sign is the Convention's catch-all, but the text names one oddly specific use: tracks where **trains move very slowly** and a railway worker walks with them, signalling to road users by hand. Think of a freight line running through a port or factory area. Countries can also add a text panel under the exclamation mark to explain the hazard, or design a new symbol that fits the system.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Which of these designs are legal danger warning signs under the Convention?

options.text: A triangle, point up, white background, red border
A triangle, point up, yellow background, red border
A yellow square standing on one corner, with a black rim
A red octagon with a white symbol
A blue circle with a white symbol

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a black arrow curving to the left.
images.caption: Model Aa: the triangle, here warning of a left bend. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-1a-V1.svg).

images.alt: A yellow diamond with a thin black rim and a black arrow curving to the left.
images.caption: Model Ab: the diamond, with the same left-bend symbol. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Ab-1a-V1.svg).

questions.explanation: The Convention offers two designs for warning signs. **Model Aa** is the red-bordered triangle with a white or yellow background. **Model Ab** is a yellow diamond with a black rim, familiar if you've driven in the Americas. Each country must pick one model for its whole territory and tell the UN Secretary-General which one it chose. The red octagon is reserved for STOP, and a blue circle is a mandatory sign.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Each member country tells the UN which warning-sign design it uses. Of those that have, which one chose the yellow diamond?

options.text: Chile
Sweden
Ireland
The United States

images.alt: A yellow diamond with a thin black rim and a black leaping deer.
images.caption: The diamond version of the wild-animals warning. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Ab-15b-V1.svg).

questions.explanation: In the UN Treaty Collection's list of these choices, **Chile** is the only country registered with the diamond; all the others registered the triangle. Road signs in South America mix Vienna Convention and US styles, so the diamond fits right in. Sweden uses triangles, just with a yellow background. Ireland uses diamonds but has never signed the Convention, and the United States isn't a member either. Chile later rejected the 2025 amendments, too.
questions.references: [UN Treaty Collection: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, status and designations](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XI-B-20&chapter=11&Temp=mtdsg3&lang=en)

questions.title: This Irish sign warns of children. Why does it look more American than European?

images.alt: A yellow diamond-shaped sign with a black rim, showing two black figures of children walking, one carrying a school bag.
images.caption: Irish road sign W 141. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IE_road_sign_W-141.svg).

options.text: Ireland never signed the Vienna Convention and has used diamond warnings since 1956
Ireland ratified the Convention and chose the diamond model
It is a temporary school-term sign, not a permanent warning
Ireland copied the design from the United Kingdom

questions.explanation: Ireland, like Iceland and Malta, has never signed the Convention. It brought in yellow diamond warnings with its 1956 traffic sign rules, twelve years before the Vienna Convention, and kept them. The pictures inside still look European: these children are closer to the figures on continental triangles than to American ones. The UK can't be the source either, because British warning signs are red-bordered triangles.
questions.references:
[Wikipedia: Road signs in Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_signs_in_Ireland)

[Wikipedia: Comparison of European road signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_European_road_signs)

questions.title: What does this sign require of you?

images.alt: A white triangle pointing downward with a thick red border and nothing inside.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B1-V1.svg).

options.text: Give way to traffic on the road you are entering, stopping only if you need to
Stop completely, even if the road is clear
You have priority at the next junction
The road narrows ahead

questions.explanation: The upside-down triangle means **Give Way**: let vehicles on the road you're joining go first. In the Convention, giving way means you don't pull out or keep going if that could force other drivers to suddenly change direction or speed. If the road is clear, you can roll through without stopping, which is the main difference from STOP. Remember the shape, though: one well-known country uses it for something else.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: It's 3 a.m., the crossroads is clearly empty, and there's a STOP sign. What does the Convention require?

options.text: Stop anyway, then give way
Slow right down, and stop only if traffic is coming
Stop only if a stop line is painted
Proceed, because STOP signs are only binding by day

questions.explanation: At a STOP sign, drivers **must stop** before entering the intersection **and** give way. An empty road is no exception. The Convention also tells authorities to use STOP instead of Give Way where drivers need to stop, especially where it's hard to see the road they're joining. So a STOP sign also hints that the junction may be harder to see than it looks.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Which inscriptions may a Convention STOP sign carry?

options.text: The English word STOP
The word for stop in the country's own language
A pictogram of a raised hand, with no words
Nothing, because the octagon alone is enough

images.alt: A red octagon with a thin white rim and the word STOP in large white letters.
images.caption: The octagonal STOP sign as drawn in the Convention. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B2a.svg).

questions.explanation: The octagonal STOP sign shows the word "STOP" in white, **in English or in the country's own language**. The letters must be at least a third of the sign's height. Across most of Europe the sign just says STOP, since many languages, French among them, borrowed the word long ago. Countries outside the Convention make other choices: Quebec uses *ARRÊT* or STOP, and Israel uses a raised-hand pictogram with no word at all. Unlike Give Way, a Convention STOP sign is never blank.
questions.references:
[United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

[Wikipedia: Stop sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_sign)

questions.title: Is this a legal STOP sign under the 1968 Convention?

images.alt: A white disc with a red ring. Inside, a red-outlined triangle points downward, with the word STOP in black near the top.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B2b-V1.svg).

options.text: Yes: it is the circular alternative, which a handful of countries chose
No: it is a Give Way sign with a text label added
No: it is an older design that the Convention banned
Yes, but only at railway level crossings

questions.explanation: The Convention has two STOP designs: the red **octagon** and this **circle**, a red-ringed disc with an empty Give Way triangle inside and STOP written above it. Each member country tells the UN which design it uses. Most chose the octagon, but the UN's list shows Bahrain, Cuba, Pakistan, San Marino, and Senegal with the circle. If you only know the octagon, this one can catch you out.
questions.references: [UN Treaty Collection: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, status and designations](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XI-B-20&chapter=11&Temp=mtdsg3&lang=en)

questions.title: You are driving in Japan. What does this red triangle pointing down mean?

images.alt: A solid red triangle pointing downward with a white rim and three white Japanese characters.
images.caption: Japanese road sign 330, as designed from 1963 to 2017. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Japan_road_sign_330-B.svg).

images.alt: A solid red downward triangle with the Japanese word for stop and, below it, the English word STOP.
images.caption: Since 2017 the sign also says STOP in English. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Japan_road_sign_330-A.svg).

options.text: Stop
Give way
Slow down
No entry

questions.explanation: The characters read 止まれ, *tomare*, which means **stop**. Japan hasn't joined the Convention. Since 1963 it has used a solid red upside-down triangle for STOP, the shape Convention countries use for Give Way. Visitors who roll through expecting to give way can get caught out. Before the 2020 Olympics, Japan considered switching to the octagon, but it kept the triangle and, from 2017, added the English word STOP.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Road signs in Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_signs_in_Japan)

questions.title: What does this sign tell you about the intersections ahead?

images.alt: A white square standing on one corner, with a thin black rim and a smaller yellow square in the centre.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B3-V1.svg).

images.alt: The same white-and-yellow diamond crossed by a black diagonal band.
images.caption: End of priority road. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B4-V1.svg).

options.text: You are on a priority road, and traffic from side roads must give way to you
Give way to traffic coming from the right
A dangerous crossroads is ahead
You are entering a toll road

questions.explanation: The yellow diamond is the **Priority Road** sign. At intersections along this road, drivers coming from other roads face Give Way or STOP signs and must let you go first. The sign may be repeated after each intersection. Your priority lasts until you see the same diamond crossed by a black band, the **End of Priority** sign. After that, the general priority rule or other signs apply again.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: You reach a narrow bridge and see this sign. You're travelling in the direction of the upward arrow. Who goes first?

images.alt: A white disc with a red ring. Inside, a black arrow points down and a red arrow points up.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B5-V1.svg).

images.alt: A blue rectangle with a white arrow pointing up and a red arrow pointing down.
images.caption: Drivers at the other end see this blue sign: priority over oncoming traffic. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_B6.svg).

options.text: Oncoming traffic; you wait until you can cross without making them stop
You do, because your arrow is the coloured one
Whoever reaches the bridge first
Nobody; the sign means the bridge is closed

questions.explanation: On this sign, the **black** arrow shows the direction that has priority and the **red** arrow shows the direction that must wait. Your arrow is red, so don't enter the narrow section if that would force oncoming drivers to stop. At the far end, drivers see a blue rectangle with a white arrow pointing up, the Convention's sign for priority over oncoming traffic. On both signs, red marks the direction that waits.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: A Give Way triangle has a small panel underneath showing the word STOP and 150 m. What does it mean?

options.text: A STOP sign is 150 m ahead
Give way now, then stop within the next 150 m
Stopping is prohibited for the next 150 m
Queues regularly stop traffic for 150 m

questions.explanation: To warn you that a STOP sign is coming, the Convention uses the **Give Way triangle** with a panel underneath showing STOP and the distance. A Give Way triangle with only a distance on its panel warns of a Give Way sign ahead. So if you see a Give Way triangle on an open road with no junction in sight, it's telling you what's waiting at the next one. The Convention also allows a red-bordered warning triangle with the STOP sign inside for the same job.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does this plain sign prohibit?

images.alt: A white disc with a wide red ring and nothing inside.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C2-V1.svg).

images.alt: A solid red disc with a horizontal white bar.
images.caption: No entry: you may not enter from this end, but traffic may still come the other way. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C1a-V1.svg).

options.text: All vehicles, in both directions
Entry from this end only, because the road is one-way
Nothing; it is a blank sign waiting for a symbol
Stopping and parking

questions.explanation: An empty red ring means the road is **closed to all vehicles in both directions**. It's easy to mix up with the red disc with a white bar, which means **No Entry**. No Entry only stops you entering from your end, usually the exit of a one-way street, so traffic can still come towards you. The empty ring closes the road to everyone, from either end.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does this sign ban?

images.alt: A blue disc with a red ring and a red X across it.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C19.svg).

images.alt: A blue disc with a red ring and a single red diagonal bar.
images.caption: One bar bans parking only. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C18.svg).

options.text: Standing and parking, so no stopping at all
Parking only; a quick stop is fine
Entry for all vehicles
U-turns

questions.explanation: A blue background inside a red ring is only used for stopping and parking rules. **One bar** means no parking. **Two bars forming an X** mean no standing *and* no parking, so you can't even stop briefly at the kerb. Either way, the ban covers only the side of the road where the sign stands, from the sign to the next junction, unless a panel says otherwise.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does this sign cancel?

images.alt: A white disc with a thin black rim and a broad black diagonal band running from upper right to lower left.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C17a-V1-1.svg).

options.text: All local prohibitions on moving vehicles, such as speed limits and overtaking bans
Every restriction, including parking and stopping bans
The priority road
Nothing; it warns that the road is closed ahead

questions.explanation: This sign has a long official name: **End of All Local Prohibitions Imposed on Moving Vehicles**. It cancels the speed limits and overtaking bans set by earlier signs. After it, the country's normal rules for that type of road apply again. It doesn't cover parking, which has its own end signs. Note the direction of the band: it runs from upper right to lower left, while a red prohibition bar runs from upper left to lower right.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Under this sign, which road users may you still overtake?

images.alt: A white disc with a red ring. Inside, a red car and a black car sit side by side.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C13aa-V1.svg).

options.text: A cyclist
A two-wheeled moped
A motorcycle without a sidecar
A slow tractor
A car doing 40 km/h below the limit

questions.explanation: The sign bans overtaking **power-driven vehicles other than two-wheeled mopeds and two-wheeled motorcycles without a sidecar**. A bicycle has no engine, so the sign doesn't cover it. A tractor does, however slow it is, so you can't overtake it, or a slow car either. National law can be stricter, and passing a cyclist still needs a safe gap. A separate version showing a lorry only stops goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes from overtaking.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: You pass a no-overtaking sign, and no end sign ever follows. Where does the ban end by default?

options.text: At the next intersection
After one kilometre
At the next town sign
Never, until an end sign appears

questions.explanation: Signs that ban or restrict something apply from where they stand **until a sign ends the rule, or else until the next intersection**. If the rule should carry on past a junction, the sign is repeated. There are two exceptions. A sign placed together with a town's entry sign applies throughout the built-up area, and a zone sign covers every road in the zone until you pass its exit sign.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: This German sign has no red slash through the bicycle. What does it mean?

images.alt: A white disc with a wide red ring and a black bicycle inside. There is no diagonal bar.
images.caption: German road sign 254. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Zeichen_254_-_Verbot_f%C3%BCr_Radfahrer,_StVO_1992.svg).

images.alt: A white disc with a red ring and a red diagonal bar across a black bicycle.
images.caption: The Convention's drawing adds a slash, but the slash is optional. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C3c-V1-1.svg).

options.text: No entry for cycles
Cycle route: bicycles welcome
Cyclists must use this road
Bicycle parking

questions.explanation: The red ring alone says "no". The Convention lets countries **leave out the red diagonal bar** on its "no entry for …" signs, or draw it unbroken where it crosses the symbol, and Germany leaves it out. The opposite message comes on a blue disc with a white bicycle: a compulsory cycle track.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: You can't read either word on this sign. What does it tell you to do?

images.alt: A white disc with a red ring and a black horizontal bar across the middle. The word DOUANE is above the bar and ZOLL below it.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C16-V1_%28Customs-FR-DE%29.svg).

options.text: Stop, because passing without stopping is prohibited here, usually at customs
No entry for foreign vehicles
Toll road ahead; payment by card only
The border crossing is closed

questions.explanation: This sign means **Passing Without Stopping Prohibited**. The Convention's version names the reason for the stop, usually *Customs*, ideally in two languages. Here the words are French *douane* and German *Zoll*, a pairing you'd expect at a border between French- and German-speaking areas. The same sign can give other reasons, such as police or a toll. Even if you can't read either word, the red ring tells you it's an order.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: On which days is parking banned on the side of the street with this sign?

images.alt: A blue disc with a red ring and a red diagonal bar, with a white Roman numeral I in the middle.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C20a.svg).

images.alt: The same blue parking sign with a white Roman numeral II.
images.caption: The II version bans parking on even-numbered dates. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_C20b.svg).

options.text: Odd-numbered dates
Even-numbered dates
Mondays only
The first half of each month

questions.explanation: These are **alternate parking** signs. With I, you can't park on that side on **odd-numbered dates**. With II, you can't park there on even-numbered dates. Cars switch sides, so the street can be cleaned. National law sets the time of the switch, which isn't always midnight. Countries can also use other periods, writing something like 1–15 and 16–31 instead of I and II.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does this blue disc with a number mean?

images.alt: A solid blue disc with a large white number 50.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D7.svg).

images.alt: The same blue disc with the number 50, crossed by a red diagonal bar.
images.caption: End of compulsory minimum speed. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D8.svg).

options.text: Minimum speed: you must drive at 50 or faster
Maximum speed: 50
Recommended speed: 50
Next exit in 50 km

questions.explanation: The colour changes the meaning. A number in a red ring is a maximum. A number on a blue disc is a mandatory sign, so it's a **compulsory minimum speed**, in the country's usual unit. Where the minimum ends, you'll see the same disc with a red bar across it. A recommended speed looks different again: the Convention shows it on a rectangular information sign, not a disc.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: This sign makes snow chains compulsory. On at least how many driving wheels must they be fitted?

images.alt: A solid blue disc with a white drawing of a tyre wrapped in snow chains.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D9a.svg).

questions.explanation: This is the Snow Chains Compulsory sign: vehicles on the road must have chains on **at least two of their driving wheels**. Chains on wheels that don't drive the car don't count, because the point is grip. You'll often see this sign at the foot of mountain passes, where the Convention's Road Open or Closed board can show it while the pass is open.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: What does the vertical line down the middle of this sign tell cyclists and pedestrians?

images.alt: A blue disc split by a white vertical line. On the left, a white bicycle; on the right, a white adult walking with a child.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D11aa.svg).

images.alt: A blue disc with a white adult and child walking above a white bicycle, with no dividing line.
images.caption: Stacked symbols mean a shared path. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_D11ba.svg).

options.text: Each group must keep to its own side of the path
Both groups may use the whole path together
Cyclists must dismount and walk
Cyclists have priority over pedestrians

questions.explanation: The layout of the symbols tells you the rule. When they sit **side by side with a line between them**, cyclists and pedestrians must each use their own side, and the two sides must be clearly separated by a kerb or road markings. When they're **stacked one above the other**, both groups share the whole path. So on a split path, walking on the cycling half breaks the rule.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: This motorway sign is green, but in some countries it is blue. Which colour does the Convention require?

images.alt: A green rectangle with a white pictogram of a divided road passing under a bridge.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_E5a-V2.svg).

images.alt: The same motorway pictogram in white on a blue rectangle.
images.caption: The blue version is just as legal. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_E5a-V1.svg).

options.text: Either: motorway signs may have a blue or a green ground
Only blue; green is for ordinary roads
Only green; blue marks the end of the motorway
Neither; motorway signs must be white

questions.explanation: The Motorway sign and motorway direction signs are **white on blue or white on green**, and each country chooses one. Germany uses blue for its motorways. Sweden introduced green for motorways around 1978, following the Convention's idea that motorways should stand out, and uses blue for ordinary roads. So the same colour can mean different road types on either side of a border. Trust the pictogram, not the paint.
questions.references:
[United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

[Wikipedia: Road signs in Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_signs_in_Sweden)

questions.title: From what length, in metres, must a tunnel have this Tunnel sign?

images.alt: A blue rectangle containing a white panel with a black tunnel-mouth pictogram.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_E11a.svg).

questions.explanation: The **Tunnel** sign marks where a tunnel's special traffic rules begin. It's required for tunnels **1,000 m or longer**, and countries may use it for shorter ones too. On those long tunnels, the length appears at the bottom of the sign or on a panel below it, and an End of Tunnel sign can show where the rules stop. These signs were part of the tunnel-safety changes added to the Convention in 2003.
questions.references:
[United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

[Wikipedia: Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Convention_on_Road_Signs_and_Signals)

questions.title: How far does the speed limit on this sign reach?

images.alt: A white rectangular panel with a speed-limit disc showing 30 and the word ZONE underneath.
images.caption: German road sign 274.1. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Zeichen_274.1_-_Beginn_einer_Tempo_30-Zone,_StVO_2013.svg).

options.text: Every road in the zone, until a sign marks the way out
Only until the next intersection
Only along this one street
Only during school hours

questions.explanation: A sign on a light rectangular panel, often with the word ZONE, applies to **every road inside the zone**. It stands on every road leading in, and at the way out you'll see the same sign greyed out with a diagonal band. This replaces the usual rule that a restriction ends at the next intersection. This German example sets up a 30 km/h zone.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: How does this blue sign differ from the red-bordered pedestrian triangle?

images.alt: A blue square with a white triangle, point up, containing a black figure walking across a striped crossing.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_E12aa-V1.svg).

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with a black figure walking across a striped crossing.
images.caption: The red-bordered warning version appears before the crossing. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-12a-V1.svg).

options.text: It marks the crossing itself, while the red triangle warns of one ahead
It is the same warning, used only in towns
It means pedestrians are banned from crossing
It marks a pedestrian-only street

questions.explanation: The symbol is the same, but the job is different. The blue square is a special regulation sign that shows pedestrians and drivers **where the crossing is**. The red-bordered triangle is a danger warning placed **before** a crossing, which itself is marked by road markings or the blue sign. The Convention also allows a blue pentagon version and one with a dark background.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: You cross a border and see this board. What does the middle row mean?

images.alt: A tall sign with a blue frame headed FRANCE and three white rows: a 50 disc beside a town silhouette; an 80 disc beside a town silhouette with a red slash; a 120 disc beside a motorway pictogram.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_G14-V1-1.svg).

options.text: 80 is the general limit outside built-up areas
80 applies for the first kilometre after leaving a town
80 is the minimum speed on rural roads
80 is the limit when it rains

questions.explanation: The **General Speed Limits** board stands near borders and sums up a country's default limits in a fixed order: in built-up areas, outside built-up areas, and on motorways. A town silhouette with a red slash is how the Convention draws "outside a built-up area". The numbers sit in red rings, so they're maximums. The figures on the Convention's drawing are just an example; the real board at each border shows that country's current limits.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: In a country that doesn't use the Latin alphabet, how must place names appear on direction signs?

options.text: In the national language plus a Latin-alphabet transliteration that follows local pronunciation
In the national language plus an English translation
In the national language only
As pictograms instead of words

questions.explanation: The Convention requires the national language plus a **transliteration into the Latin alphabet** that matches the local pronunciation as closely as possible. The Latin version can go on the same sign or on a second sign. Transliteration spells out the sound instead of translating the name, so a sign for Москва reads *Moskva*, not *Moscow*. One more rule: no sign may carry text in more than two languages.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)

questions.title: Which of these countries signed the Convention in 1968 but never ratified it?

options.text: United Kingdom
Spain
Brazil
Germany
France
Sweden

questions.explanation: Signing a treaty shows a country intends to join; **ratifying** it makes the treaty binding. The UK, Spain, and Brazil all signed in Vienna on 8 November 1968 but never ratified, so they aren't among the 75 parties. British and Spanish signs still look very European. France ratified in 1971, Germany in 1978, and Sweden in 1985. The Convention came into force on 6 June 1978, after 15 countries had ratified it.
questions.references: [UN Treaty Collection: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, status and designations](https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XI-B-20&chapter=11&Temp=mtdsg3&lang=en)

questions.title: A 2025 amendment to the Convention takes effect on 12 November 2026. How did it become binding without each country voting to ratify it?

options.text: Fewer than one-third of the parties objected within 12 months, so it was deemed accepted
A two-thirds majority approved it at a conference in Vienna
The UN Security Council imposed it
Every party signed it individually

questions.explanation: Under Article 41, amendments can pass by **tacit acceptance**, where silence counts as a yes. The proposal goes round for twelve months, and if fewer than a third of the parties reject it, it counts as accepted. Six months later it takes effect for everyone except the countries that objected. The 2025 package, which brings a new way of numbering the signs, cleared that bar in May 2026. Chile and the Netherlands rejected it and stay on the old text. A conference with a two-thirds vote is only the backup route.
questions.references:
[UN depositary notification C.N.170.2026: acceptance of amendments (PDF)](https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/CN/2026/CN.170.2026-Eng.pdf)

[Wikipedia: Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Convention_on_Road_Signs_and_Signals)

questions.title: In what kind of country would you expect to see this roundabout warning?

images.alt: A red-bordered white triangle with three black arrows chasing each other clockwise around a circle.
images.caption: Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-22-V1-LHT.svg).

images.alt: The same roundabout warning with the arrows running anticlockwise.
images.caption: The right-hand-traffic original, arrows anticlockwise. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vienna_Convention_road_sign_Aa-22-V1.svg).

options.text: One where traffic drives on the left
One where traffic drives on the right
Any country, because the arrow direction is decorative
Only at motorway junctions

questions.explanation: The arrows run **clockwise**, the way traffic goes round a roundabout in countries that drive on the left. A note covering the Convention's whole sign annex says that in those countries, signs and symbols are reversed where needed. Member countries such as India, Pakistan, and Cyprus drive on the left, so their bend, roundabout, and lane arrows are mirrored. The shapes and colours stay the same.
questions.references: [United Nations: Convention on Road Signs and Signals, consolidated text (PDF)](https://www.makinggood.ac.nz/media/1274/un_conv_road_signs_2006.pdf)
